newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe black empowerment lobby keeps up pressure.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe black empowerment lobby keeps up pressure.

text.p: Black Zimbabwean pressure groups are campaigning hard to wrest economic power from white-run businesses, but political analysts say there are no signs that the government is ready to adopt their policies.
Phillip Chiyangwa, president of the Affirmative Action Group (AAG), met President Robert Mugabe in a highly publicised closed-door meeting last week on "economic liberation".

The AAG, the Indigenous Business Development Centre (IBDC), the Indigenous Business Women's Organisation and some top ruling ZANU-PF party officials are trying to lessen the clout of big "white" corporations, who control about 80 percent of business.
Whites also control 60 percent of the country's most fertile farm land, but they insist that they have been taking on black partners in new business ventures.
The black lobby accuses whites of running the national economy like a cartel and says some blacks -- labelled as Uncle Toms -- have undermined efforts by Zimbabwean blacks to get access to finance.

Its sweeping attacks are drummed up in Zimbabwe's dominant state media, which regularly accuses whites -- about one percent of the southern African country's 10.5 million people -- of not doing enough to promote blacks in 17 years of independence.
But few blacks are impressed by the state media's rhetoric, seen by some political analysts as a smokescreen by a few to enrich themselves in the name of the majority.

They point to the lack of a clear government programme and say that top state officials have grabbed for themselves most of the land acquired from white commercial farmers for mass resettlement programmes.

"Everyone wishes there was some programme, but there is none," said John Makumbe, a political science lecturer at Harare's University of Zimbabwe. "The governmemt's plans are vague at the moment and what we are seeing don't pass for clear programmes. They just allow a few people to prosper."

Makumbe said even Mugabe -- who regularly endorses the IBDC and the AAG's attacks that many whites are racists dedicated to keeping blacks poor -- has been moving very slowly on the black empowerment path.
"Many people think it has been hijacked by some people and some politicians...I don't get the impression, he is going to implement the proposals he has been getting wholesomely," he said.
The IBDC is daily pressing Mugabe to adopt a plan it submitted to him last December, urging him to invoke special presidential powers to launch a comprehensive black empowerment programme.
The IBDC recommendations include calls on the government to:

- implement a long-standing promise to forcibly acquire more massive tracts of white-owned land to resettle black peasants and those willing to try commercial farming; forbid foreign mining companies from mineral exploration and to ensure the exceptions give local black investors a 61 percent stake in their projects;
- order pension funds in the country to direct at least 30 percent of their investment funds towards black businesses;
- make it difficult for foreign and local white investors to go into Zimbabwe's urban and commercial transport sector while offering state assistance to blacks seeking to do the same;
- enact laws that favour blacks who were discriminated against before Zimbabwe won black majority rule in 1980; award them business contracts and be generous and lenient to their failures.
Charles Rukuni, publisher of a Zimbabwean monthly political newsletter The Insider, said a solid programme may take months to assemble, but meantime the rhetoric would continue.
